parts.title: Type inference, or how TypeScript decides a variable's type

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 2 - TypeScript - Type inference, or how TypeScript decides a variable's type

TypeScript works out the type of a variable from the value you give it. In
[Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1), every variable had its type written out so you
could see it. TypeScript can work the type out from the value, and from now on the course leaves it
out. This lesson shows why that is safe.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Type inference, which is how TypeScript works out the type of a variable from its value. |
| **Goals** | Explain why `const box = page.locator('#checkbox1')` needs no type written after it, and name the two places where a type is still written by hand. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1), where every variable had its type written out. |
| **Tools** | `const`, `console.log`, and `page.locator()`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right. The Console tab shows what your code prints. |
| **Key takeaway** | TypeScript reads the type from the value, so a variable made from a value needs no annotation. |

## 1. Where a type comes from

[Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1) wrote `const name: string = 'Leela'`. The
`: string` part is a **type annotation**, which is the type written out by hand after the name.
TypeScript does not need it. It reads the value on the right of `=`, and gives the variable the
type of that value. This is called **type inference**, and it means that `'Leela'` makes `name` a
`string` whether or not `: string` is written.

The example below creates three variables without an annotation, and prints them. Select
**Load into editor**, then select **Run**:

```ts
// No type is written. TypeScript gives each name the type of its value.
const name = 'Leela';
const age = 30;
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}`;

console.log(name);
console.log(age + 1);
console.log(greeting);
```

**Output**

```output
Leela
31
Hello, Leela
```

**Explanation:** `name` is a `string`, because `'Leela'` is text. `age` is a `number`, because
`30` is a number, which is why `age + 1` is `31`. `greeting` is a `string`, because a template
literal always produces text. The types are as fixed as they were in Week 1. If a later line tried
to put a number into `name`, TypeScript would report an error, with or without the annotation.

In VS Code, hovering the mouse over a name shows the type that TypeScript gave it, such as
`const name: string`.

## 2. The same rule for a locator

A locator is a value too, so the rule is the same. When you write:

```ts
const box = page.locator('#checkbox1');
```

`page.locator()` returns a `Locator`, so TypeScript gives `box` the type `Locator`. Nothing in
[Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2) writes `: Locator` after a variable name, because TypeScript has
already worked it out. The type still does its job. If you spelled a method wrong, such as
`box.chekc()`, VS Code would underline it before the test ran.

Two places in this course still write a type by hand, and for the same reason. A function
parameter, such as `email: string` in `fillRegistrationForm(page: Page, email: string)`, has no
value yet when the function is written. A class property, such as `readonly emailField: Locator`
in [Week 1 - Day 5 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3), is declared before the constructor gives it
a value. In both places, there is no value to read, so there is nothing to infer from.
`const age = 30;` has no type written after `age`. What type does TypeScript give it?

options: `number`, because the value on the right of `=` is a number
`string`, because a value without an annotation is treated as text
None until the code runs, because a type applies only once it is written out
checkpoint.explanation: TypeScript reads the value `30`, which is a number, and gives `age` the type `number`. The type is fixed before the code runs, as it was with the annotation in Week 1. Leaving the annotation out changes what you write, not what TypeScript checks.

blocks.text: Why does the course write `email: string` in `fillRegistrationForm(page: Page, email: string)`, but no `: Locator` in `const box = page.locator('#checkbox1')`?

options: A parameter has no value yet, so there is nothing to infer from
A locator has no type of its own, so there is nothing that could be written after it
A parameter is checked more strictly than a variable, so its type must be spelled out
checkpoint.explanation: Inference reads a type from a value. A parameter is written before any value is passed in, so its type must be written by hand. `box` is given a value at once, and `page.locator()` returns a `Locator`, so TypeScript reads that type without help.

blocks.text: You write `const box = page.locator('#checkbox1')` and then `box.chekc()` in VS Code. What happens?

options: VS Code underlines `chekc`, because a `Locator` has no such method
Nothing, because a variable without an annotation is not checked
The test runs and fails, because the mistake is found only when the line runs
checkpoint.explanation: TypeScript gave `box` the type `Locator` by inference, and a `Locator` has `check` but no `chekc`, so VS Code reports the error before the test runs. A missing annotation does not switch checking off, because the type was read from the value.

blocks.text:
- **Type inference** is TypeScript reading a variable's type from the value on the right of `=`.
- `const name = 'Leela'` is a `string`, and `const box = page.locator('#checkbox1')` is a `Locator`, without either type being written.
- A function parameter and a class property still write their types by hand, because neither has a value to read yet.

## What's next

[Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2) writes locators by hand with `page.locator()`, and adds three
assertions to the one you know.

parts.title: XPath, CSS, and three more assertions

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 2 - Fundamentals - XPath, CSS, and three more assertions

An assertion decides whether a test passes, and a locator decides which element the assertion
looks at. [Week 1 - Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) wrote one assertion, `toHaveURL`. This
lesson adds three more, `toHaveValue`, `toContainText`, and `toHaveText`, and two ways of writing
a locator by hand for an element that has no role, label, or placeholder to find it by.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Two ways of writing a locator by hand, and three assertions that check a value or a text. |
| **Goals** | Write a CSS selector and an XPath for the same element, read a field's value and an element's text, and assert on them with `toHaveValue`, `toContainText`, and `toHaveText`. |
| **Prerequisites** | [TypeScript](/learn/w2/d2/p1) for type inference, and [Week 1 - Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) for `expect` and `toHaveURL`. |
| **Tools** | `page.locator()`, `count()`, `inputValue()`, `textContent()`, `toHaveValue`, `toContainText`, and `toHaveText`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the locators, then your own project for the assertions, because `expect` needs the test runner. |
| **Scope** | This lesson names an attribute in an XPath. XPath steps that move to a neighboring element are covered in [Day 4 - Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d4/p2). |
| **Key takeaway** | A field holds a value and an element holds text, and each matcher checks one of the two. |

## Two ways to write a locator by hand

[Day 1 - Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d1/p2) used `page.locator()` for the fields on the registration
form that have no placeholder, such as the email field. `page.locator()` takes a piece of text that
describes an element by how the page is built. That text can be written in one of two languages.

A **CSS selector** is a short pattern that names an element by its tag, its id, or one of its
attributes. An **attribute** is a named setting written inside a tag, such as `type='email'` inside
`<input type='email'>`. An **id** is an attribute that gives one element a name of its own, which
no other element on the page should share.

**XPath** is a second language for the same job. It describes a path to an element through the
page, and it can name an attribute along the way.

| To find | CSS selector | XPath |
|---|---|---|
| The button whose id is `Button1` | `#Button1` | `//button[@id='Button1']` |
| The input whose `type` attribute is `email` | `input[type='email']` | `//input[@type='email']` |

The pieces of each pattern:

| Piece | Language | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `#` | CSS | The id that follows | `#Button1` finds the element whose id is `Button1` |
| `tag[attr='value']` | CSS | An element with that tag, whose attribute has that value | `input[type='tel']` finds the phone field |
| `//` | XPath | Anywhere on the page | `//input` finds every input, wherever it is |
| `[ ]` | XPath | A condition that the element must meet | `//button[@id='submitbtn']` finds the button whose id is `submitbtn` |
| `@` | XPath | The attribute that follows | `@placeholder='First Name'` means the placeholder is `First Name` |

[Week 1 - Day 4 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2) said that XPath breaks when the layout changes.
That was true of the example it showed, `//div[3]/button[1]`, which means the first button inside
the third `div`. An XPath like that describes a position, so moving the button breaks it. An XPath
that names an attribute, such as `//button[@id='Button1']`, finds the button wherever it is. It
survives a redesign in the same way that a CSS selector does.

Both languages are still a second choice. When an element has a role and a name, or a placeholder,
`getByRole` and `getByPlaceholder` describe what the user sees, and they come first.

variation.prompt: Find the First Name field twice, once with an XPath that names its placeholder attribute, and once with a CSS selector that names the same attribute. Print the count of each. Both should print 1.

blocks.text:
## What a failing assertion looks like Change `'Register'` to `'Sign up'` in the last assertion, and run the same command again: ```bash npx playwright test tests/register-assertions.spec.ts --project=chromium ``` **Output** ```output Running 1 test using 1 worker 1) [chromium] › tests\register-assertions.spec.ts:3:5 › the registration page shows its headings and keeps a typed email Error: expect(locator).toHaveText(expected) failed Locator: locator('h2') Expected: "Sign up" Received: "Register" Timeout: 5000ms Call log: - Expect "toHaveText" locator('h2') with timeout 5000ms - waiting for locator('h2') 14 × locator resolved to

Register

- unexpected value "Register" 12 | // Check part of the main heading, and the whole of the form heading. 13 | await expect(page.locator('h1')).toContainText('Automation Demo'); > 14 | await expect(page.locator('h2')).toHaveText('Sign up'); | ^ 15 | }); 1 failed [chromium] › tests\register-assertions.spec.ts:3:5 › the registration page shows its headings and keeps a typed email ``` **Explanation:** The `Expected` line is what the test asked for, and the `Received` line is what the page holds. The call log shows that the assertion looked at the heading 14 times over five seconds before it gave up, which is the retrying at work. The `>` marks the line that failed. Read the `Received` line first when a test fails. If the page is right and the test is wrong, as here, change the test. In your terminal, the error also shows the full path of the spec file, and the path of a folder named `test-results` that holds details of the failure. Change `'Sign up'` back to `'Register'` before you go on.

## Best practices

- Use `getByRole`, `getByPlaceholder`, `getByLabel`, or `getByText` first, and a CSS selector or an
  XPath only when the element has none of those.
- Name an attribute in an XPath, never a position, so that the locator survives a redesign.
- Print `count()` in the editor before you use a hand-written locator in an action, and expect `1`.
- Use `toHaveValue` for a field, and `toContainText` or `toHaveText` for a heading, a message, or a
  button.
- Use `toContainText` when part of the text is enough, and `toHaveText` when the whole text matters.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Used a text matcher on a field | `expect(locator).toHaveText(expected) failed`, with `Received: ""` | A field's contents are its value, not its text. Use `toHaveValue`. |
| Acted on a locator that matches two elements, such as `page.locator("input[type='text']").fill('Ada')` | `strict mode violation: locator('input[type=\'text\']') resolved to 2 elements` | Make the pattern more precise, such as `input[placeholder='First Name']`, or use `getByPlaceholder`. |
| Wrote `@` in a CSS selector | `Unsupported token "@type" while parsing css selector` | `@` belongs to XPath. Write `input[type='email']`, or start the text with `xpath=//`. |
| Expected a value that the page does not have | `Expected: "Sign up"` above `Received: "Register"` | Read the `Received` line. It is what the page holds, and the test must expect what the page holds. |
Which XPath still finds the Refresh button after a redesign moves it to another part of the page?

options: `//div[3]/button[1]`, because it records the button's exact position
`//button[@id='Button1']`, because it names the button's own id
Neither, because every XPath depends on the layout of the page
checkpoint.explanation: An XPath that names an attribute finds the element wherever it is, because the id moves with the button. `//div[3]/button[1]` describes a position, so it finds whatever is at that position after the redesign, which is no longer the Refresh button.

blocks.text: You typed an email into a field. Which matcher checks that the field holds it?

options: `toHaveText`, because the email is text
`toHaveValue`, because a field's contents are its value
`toContainText`, because the email now appears on the page
checkpoint.explanation: What is typed into a field is its value, and `toHaveValue` checks the value. The text matchers read the text between an element's tags, and a field has none, so `toHaveText` receives an empty string and fails.

blocks.text: The `h1` text is `Automation Demo Site ` with a space at the end. Why does `toContainText('Automation Demo')` pass?

options: It checks for a part of the text, so the rest does not matter
It removes every space from both texts before comparing them
It retried until the page removed the space from the heading
checkpoint.explanation: `toContainText` passes when the piece it is given appears anywhere in the text, so neither `Site` nor the space after it is compared. The retrying never changes the page. It only gives the page time to show the text.

blocks.text:
- A **CSS selector** such as `#Button1` or `input[type='email']`, and an **XPath** such as `//button[@id='Button1']`, both describe an element by how the page is built.
- An XPath that names an attribute survives a redesign. One that records a position, such as `//div[3]/button[1]`, does not.
- `toHaveValue` checks what a field holds. `toContainText` checks for part of an element's text, and `toHaveText` checks the whole of it.
- A failed assertion prints an `Expected` line and a `Received` line, and the `Received` line is what the page holds.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w2/d2/p3) places the three assertions in a helper function, next to
`fillRegistrationForm`, so that every registration test can call them.

parts.title: The same assertions, in a helper every test can call

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 2 - Implementation - The same assertions, in a helper every test can call

In [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2), the assertions sat inside one test. In this lesson, you place
the checks that every registration test needs in one function, next to `fillRegistrationForm` from
[Day 1 - Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3). You do every step in VS Code and in its integrated
terminal, in your own project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Placing the checks that every registration test needs in one helper function. |
| **Goals** | Add `expectFormFilled` to the helper file, call it from two tests, and explain when a helper may contain an assertion. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2) for the three matchers, and [Day 1 - Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3) for `fillRegistrationForm`. |
| **Tools** | `export`, `expect`, `toHaveValue`, and `import` from a file of your own. |
| **Environment** | VS Code and its integrated terminal, in your project folder. |
| **Key takeaway** | A function either performs actions or asserts, and never does both. |

## The problem with the Fundamentals version

Imagine ten tests that each fill the registration form and then check that the form holds the
values. Each test repeats the same three `expect` lines. If the email field changes, you edit ten
tests. [Day 1 - Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3) solved the same problem for the actions, by
writing them once in `fillRegistrationForm`. The checks get the same treatment.

## When a helper may contain an assertion

[Week 1 - Day 5 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3) gave a rule: a page object performs actions and
contains no assertions, so that tests expecting different results can all use it. `expectFormFilled`
seems to break that rule. It does not, because it is a different kind of helper. Its whole job is
to assert, and its name says so.

The rule to keep is that one function never does both. `fillRegistrationForm` fills the form and
checks nothing. `expectFormFilled` checks the form and fills nothing. A test that needs a different
check calls `fillRegistrationForm` on its own, and writes its own assertion. A test that needs the
usual check calls both.

## Why it is shaped this way

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| The checks are in `registration-helpers.ts`, not in the spec file | Every test that fills the form can call them, and a changed locator is edited once. |
| The name starts with `expect` | A reader of a test sees at once that the line checks the page and does not change it. |
| The email is a parameter, and the other values are fixed | The email is the only value that `fillRegistrationForm` varies, so it is the only one the checker needs to be told. |
| Filling and checking are two functions, not one | A test can fill the form and then check something else, or check nothing, without changing the helper. |

## What a reviewer looks for

- Repeated `expect` lines live in one function, not in every test.
- A function that asserts is named for it, with `expect` at the start of its name.
- No function both performs actions and asserts.
Why may `expectFormFilled` contain assertions, when the page object in Week 1 - Day 5 - Implementation could not?

options: Asserting is its whole job, and its name says so
Assertions are allowed in any function that is not part of a class
It asserts on values, and only assertions on the address are kept out of helpers
checkpoint.explanation: The rule from Week 1 keeps actions and checks apart, so that tests expecting different results can share the actions. `expectFormFilled` performs no action, and its name tells a reader that it checks. Whether a function is in a class makes no difference to the rule.

blocks.text: The website renames the email field. Three tests call `fillRegistrationForm` and `expectFormFilled`. How many places do you edit?

options: Two, one in each helper
Three, one in each test
Six, one fill and one check in each test
checkpoint.explanation: The locator for the email field is written once in `fillRegistrationForm` and once in `expectFormFilled`. The tests contain no locators, so they need no change. Without the helpers, the same rename would be six edits.

blocks.text: A new test must check something that `expectFormFilled` does not check. What does it call?

options: `fillRegistrationForm` and `expectFormFilled`, and nothing else
`fillRegistrationForm`, and then its own assertion
`expectFormFilled` with a different email, to change the check
checkpoint.explanation: Filling and checking are separate functions, so a test can fill the form with the helper and then write any assertion it needs. Passing a different email to `expectFormFilled` changes only the expected email, not what is checked.

blocks.text:
- Repeated `expect` lines are the same problem as repeated actions, and get the same fix: one function that every test calls.
- A helper whose whole job is to assert may assert, and its name starts with `expect` so that a reader can tell.
- `fillRegistrationForm` fills and checks nothing, and `expectFormFilled` checks and fills nothing. One function never does both.

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w2/d2/p4) has you write locators by hand, assert on a filled form, and read the
error that `expectFormFilled` reports when an expected value is wrong.

# Week 2 - Day 2 - Practice - XPath, CSS, and assertions

These three problems use the hand-written locators and the three matchers from
[Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2), and the `expectFormFilled` helper from
[Implementation](/learn/w2/d2/p3). The first problem runs in the editor, and the other two run in
your own project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three problems about hand-written locators and assertions, from Beginner level to Advanced. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2) for locators and matchers, and [Implementation](/learn/w2/d2/p3) for `expectFormFilled`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the first problem, and your own project for the other two. |

## How to answer

The problems come in three levels. Beginner uses one idea from the lesson, Intermediate combines
two, and Advanced asks you to read an error. Select **Start this in the editor** to open a template
for a problem, and write your answer on the lines that start with `//`. Select **Reveal solution**
to compare it with a model answer.

## When you are done

You can now find an element by an attribute in either language, check a field's value and an
element's text, and keep the checks that every test needs in one helper.
[Day 3 - TypeScript](/learn/w2/d3/p1) continues from here.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Four locators written by hand, for four elements on the registration form, and
a printed count for each. Write the Last Name field and the Submit button as XPath, using the
placeholder attribute and the id. Write the phone field and the Cricket checkbox as CSS selectors,
using the `type` attribute and the id. Print `count()` for each locator.

**Where.** In the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The Console tab shows four lines, and each one is `1`.

**Hint.** The Submit button has the id `submitbtn`, the phone field has the type `tel`, and the
Cricket checkbox has the id `checkbox1`. The first two appear in the table of pieces in
[Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2).

**What to build.** A test that fills the registration form with `fillRegistrationForm` from
[Day 1 - Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3), using the email `katy@example.com`, and then checks four
things. The email field holds that email, the Last Name field holds `Lovelace`, the Skills list
holds `Java`, and the form heading contains `Regis`. Use `toHaveValue` for the three fields and
`toContainText` for the heading. In the `tests` folder, create `practice-values.spec.ts`, write
the test, and run it.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy your test and the result into the editor,
using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The run reports `1 passed`.

**Hint.** A list made with `<select>`, such as `#Skills`, holds a value in the same way that a text
field does, so `toHaveValue('Java')` works on it. The form heading is the `h2` element.

**What to build.** A test that fills the form with `fillRegistrationForm`, using the email
`ada@example.com`, and checks it with `expectFormFilled`, using the same email. In the `tests`
folder, create `practice-checker.spec.ts`, write the test, and run it. Then change the email given
to `expectFormFilled` to `wrong@example.com`, run the test again, and copy the `Expected` line and
the `Received` line from the error.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy your test and the two lines into the
editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The first run reports `1 passed`. The second reports `1 failed`,
and the error names `registration-helpers.ts`, because the assertion that failed is inside the
helper.

**Hint.** The error shows the line inside `expectFormFilled` with a `>` next to it, and below that
the line of your test that called it.
